item.title: The Fight for Survival
item.dc:creator: robyn
item.content:encoded: It is June 10, 2015 and I'm on a game drive in the Maasai Mara with my guests from New Zealand. We find the four notorious Notch brothers resting or eating next to a hippo which they have killed only hours before we arrive. These boys are famous for killing hippo because they have the strength and numbers to do so. They don't kill in the same way as if it were a buffalo, for example. With hippo they roll it onto its back and begin eating. Shock will sort the rest. Notch ll, Ron, Caesar and Grimace are enjoying their feast. There are a handful of hyenas nearby who are watching from a safe distance. The hippo is encrusted with flies which annoy the big cats and they frequently sneeze to rid themselves of the buzzing nuisances while they eat. The boys have had their fill and move a short distance to rest.  We leave them as it's time to head back to camp for the evening. The next morning we are curious about what has happened overnight so go back to the site of the hippo kill. Caesar is the only one not there. A lioness has come in during the night with her cub. It doesn't belong to the boys and Grimace has killed it. That's the way nature works with lions. Its lifeless body lies in the grass, only a few metres from the hippo, as its mother feeds. A dozen hyenas are circling but won't come close as they fear an attack from one of the Notch boys. The lioness periodically growls and tries her best to keep them away too. Three of the hyenas move in and Notch ll takes exception, charges and chases them away. We stay for about an hour then decide to move off and continue our game drive. It isn't long before we see another lioness with ten cubs; including two sub-adults. They are headed straight for the Notches and, if they don't belong to their pride, the same fate will become these cubs. (I learn later this is the Rekero Pride and do not belong). Concerned for their safety, we turn and follow their path. The lioness is on a mission. It takes some time before they get to a point where they can now see the Notches. But the Notches can also see them. Their heads are raised but they don't move. The lioness sits down to give herself and the pride time to rest. They have the vantage point of being higher than the boys as they have come over the brow of a hill. Five of the cubs take this as a chance to play and, although it's not usual for lions to climb trees, these little guys do. It seems as though they are going to settle in here for some time so we take the opportunity to head off again and see what other animals we can find. The plan is to return later in the day and check up on the situation. Returning later in the afternoon, we find the gap between the resting place and the Notches has halved at least. The Rekero Pride are still keeping a safe distance but they are hungry. It is a mix of fear and empty bellies that drives them to this spot. The Notches are still protecting their hippo kill and aren't letting go. The pride stick together on a mound and watch............ Hunger gets the better of a few of them and, led by the juvenile male, move in closer. The juvenile gets within a few metres of the hippo and can smell his meal. Notch ll objects and charges at him chasing, not only him, but the others away to where they had previously been resting. Time to head back to camp again. But our curiosity is now growing stronger so we plan another visit in the morning. Arriving at the scene once more it's a completely different scenario. The Notches have all moved off up the hill, about an hour earlier we're told, and cannot be seen from here. Instead, the Rekero Pride have moved in on the hippo and are either resting with full bellies or still eating. To add to the mix though, there are two opposing clans of hyenas. One clan is much bigger than the other and, in the background, they are challenging each other. At this point the lions are taking no notice of them. The hunger is now getting the better of the hyenas and they know they have a good chance of getting in to feed. Together, regardless of opposing sides, they out number the lions. And most of this pride are cubs. All through this time though, both lions and hyenas are nervous. They know where the Notches went and they know at any time, they could attack. There's always someone keeping vigil in case they need to run. But there's business at hand. The juvenile male is eating on his own and the hyenas charge the hippo carcass. He stands his guard initially. He growls and snarls but is beaten back. It's in his best interest now to concede defeat. In retaliation, the lioness now comes in assisted by some of the cubs and the juvenile. There is mayhem. The hyenas attack the lions. The lions attack the hyenas. And the hyenas attack each other. The noise is incredible! No one is backing down. At the same time, all parties are conscious of staying alive, or at least, not being injured. The noise may have alerted the Notches and the vigil must continue. The spotters are keeping watch. The hyenas take over and the carcass is being shredded. ( Watch in HD and turn sound up high to hear lions) Tempers are being tested; even among the lions. There's no point in fighting. The only way forward for all is to share this meal. There is no getting cosy with each other, that is for sure. But, they take their turn and everyone is fed. It is amazing to see that this one hippo added to the survival of almost 50 other animals. And what became of the Notch boys then? The noise doesn't attract them at all. They aren't interested. We find two of them up the hill sleeping and fully sated. The following day they are all chased away by buffaloes. The Rekero Pride have all disappeared. Safely fed and in no need of food for another week. All that remains of the hippo is the skeleton of which the vultures are now picking at. The leathery skin has been shredded from the bones and is being played with by one remaining hyena. Time to move on..............!
item.excerpt:encoded: It is June 10, 2015 and I'm on a game drive in the Maasai Mara with my guests from New Zealand. We find the four notorious Notch brothers resting or eating next to a hippo which they have killed only hours before we arrive. These boys are famous for killing hippo because they have the strength and numbers to do so. They don't kill in the same way as if it were a buffalo, for example. With hippo they roll it onto its back and begin eating. Shock will sort the rest.

wp:comment.wp:comment_content: I wonder why that lioness was let to feed on the carcass of the hippo if it did not belong to the Notche's pride!This Lioness must have been a careless mother to wander with her cub to territory that is taken only for her cub to be killed and she feeds as if nothing has happened at all!Quite strange in deed!

It would appear that the lionesses were ex "wives" of the Notches. The cubs, however, were fathered by Blackie and Lipstick of the Rekero Pride so were not fathered by the Notches. Most likely the boys recognized the lionesses and let them feed. When we were sitting there, and the juvenile first made an attempt to get to the hippo, the boys chased them away. Coming back the next morning though, the Notches had moved away up the hill. They were not within eye sight of the hippo so maybe they didn't even see the pride there. The Notches were all very well fed anyway so didn't care. At the end of the day only one cub was killed when the Notches had the opportunity to kill more. And everyone got a feed. At a time when the Migration is still not there and food was scarce, and still is, many of the lion prides are moving outside their territories simply to find food to eat. And with a big pride such as Rekero, it's a mission for the lionesses.
Robyn where abouts was this sighting
Hi Matt....this was in the Mara not far from Entim Camp.

item.title: In Search of the Prince of Darkness
item.dc:creator: robyn
item.content:encoded: For five solid days (Sept 4-8 inclusive) Dedan and I were off on safari. This was not just any safari. It was a personal challenge and a mission. And what a challenge it proved to be! Where were we ? And what were we looking for? We ventured into the Laikipia region of Kenya to look for the very rare and extremely elusive melanistic (black) leopard. These cats carry a dominant gene which causes an excessive amount of melanin resulting in their black colour. In certain lights their patches can still be seen. And at night, they are almost invisible. We were permitted entry onto a private property which covered approximately 100,000 acres and, at it's highest point, sits at around 2400m. At this time we were the only people, outside of staff, allowed on the property so were able to come and go as we liked as far as game drives went. This included night drives. The landscape consisted almost entirely of thick bush and long grasses. This would become the most challenging part of this venture. My accommodation consisted of a room made from stone with a thatched roof. Even the bed base was made from stone. Using natural resources is always a good thing, right? There were gaps around the top of the beams and I did wonder if it would let small animals in. At times in the night I could hear things scratching but chose to ignore it! . A longdrop toilet and bucket shower completed the necessities. The shower being a short walk across the grass behind the room. There were two holes in the stone in the washroom area and I did wonder why they were there. Ventilation or illumination? At any rate, they were low enough to the ground that anything could have jumped in at night.  Even a sizeable cat. I managed to find something to stuff into them during dark hours.....just in case !!  Lighting was by solar power only. At night I was somewhat isolated in that, being the only one there, my room was well apart from any staff quarters. In fact several hundred metres. I did wonder at times what would happen if I was attacked by some strange creature in the dark and, if I yelled, would anyone hear me? On more than one occasion I was woken by a large herd of buffaloes surrounding my room. As in, right outside. I could hear them wrenching the grass with their teeth and grunting to each other. And, if it wasn't buffaloes, it was herds of impala barking their territorial calls. Zebras roamed there as well but at least they were silent. I guess if the buffaloes were there I was safe from anything else. Not a situation for the faint hearted. I've heard it said that Africa is no place for sissies ! There was a short walk from where we ate our meals to where my room was. On one occasion a large herd of buffaloes were only a few metres away grazing. All I had between me and them was the darkness and a torch. I could see their eyes shining as I walked and hoped they stayed where they were and saw me as no threat. Being one of the most feared animals in Africa, it was heart-in-mouth stuff. One evening we heard that a leopard had attacked the owners dogs and killed three pups. This was only a few hundred metres again from my room. I wonder if that cat also walked past my door? You never know what's lurking out there in the dark. Especially on a property where the animals roam freely. That's the best part of being in the African bush. Allowing them their rights of passage. But, at the same time, adding that extra edge of uncertainty while you're trying to sleep. Best to just get down under the covers with the hot water bottle and ponder tomorrow ! Our first game drive began at 6am on day one. Each morning and evening it was very cold. I wasn't used to that and it was lucky I'd taken my shoes and warm jacket. Even the not-worn scarf and hat got pulled out of the bag. Because of the dense vegetation it was difficult even to see any game at all. Random impalas, waterbucks, buffaloes and warthogs were all that we were able to see. The few elephants ducked back into the bushes quickly. This isn't a place where wild animals are used to traffic. This was a location Dedan and I had never been so it wasn't familiar at all. Because of that we enlisted the help of a private guide to show us around the property. And lucky we did because, without his help, we would have easily got lost. There were no landmarks. Nothing was identifiable. Everywhere looked the same....dense and rugged. The tracks were one vehicle only and, in a lot of places, sizeable rocks that made our jungle machine slide and grate as we went along. Branches bit up from underneath and, at some point, ripped the speedo cable. The sides of the vehicle constantly got lashed with the passing bushes and many a time I had to duck for cover. The first afternoon greeted us with a massive thunder storm. We had taken the afternoon off with a plan of a game drive at 5pm. In the meantime, I was confined to my room as the lightning and thunder raged directly above me. The rain poured down and I noticed four zebras out from my room huddled in a bunch. The interesting thing about these parts is, the following day, apart from puddles, you wouldn't know it had rained. The first evening game drive started at 5pm. It was still slushy from the rain and we hoped that would flush any cats out of the bushes and onto the road. Our focus, of course, was this black leopard. On arrival we had spoken with a long time staff member who knew the territories of this cat and who had also seen, possibly two or three, at various times during his employment there. He advised on locations to look to avoid driving aimlessly. Bear in mind this is a huge property so we didn't want to waste limited time. This became our focus. No luck!  We had just arrived back at camp and were standing next to the fire to warm up when the property manager arrived. He had just heard a leopard calling out opposite his house. Drop everything....we're off ! Dinner will have to wait. Two hours of patrolling in the dark but we couldn't find it. The following day we found leopard prints on the road. Easy to read when they've walked in wet earth. It was most likely standing in the dark watching us go by. When we first arrived there was some curiosity as to why we had an interest in the black leopard. We discovered that several of the staff had seen one at some point but didn't realize how rare and special they are. Suddenly they were all onboard with the idea and all asking to come out on our evening game drives. We were given advice and, on two drives, assisted by rangers to do spotting with the light. They're trained at this and their eyes pick up things that move. Using a spotlight enhances the animals' eyes and, even from a distance, you can identify what that animal is by the colour of the eyes. Night drives are a whole different experience. On two night drives we were lucky to see a civet. They were too quick for me to get any photo as they darted back into the bush. Also on two occasions, a hunting pair of Verreaux Eagle Owls. And so it continued. The days began at 6am. We ventured back to camp for lunch and took a break until 5pm. Apart from the one rainy day, the rest were scorching hot and no cat was going to be out in that. Then at 5pm we went out again until some time between 9 and10pm. Searching the tracks and bushes by day and the roads and very scarce open areas by night. If we spotted a herd of impala, who sleep in the open at night for safety, we scoured around them in the hope the leopard might be lurking nearby. Trying to see a black leopard at night time would be a mission in itself. And trying to find this rare and elusive creature by day on this property was like looking for a needle in a haystack. The best we could hope for was that it walked out in front of us. We did see a "normal" leopard, but no black one. Our days were long and, at times tiresome. The vehicle got absolutely hammered but it withstood every bump and hollow. Every crevice and valley. Every rock climb and puddle. Every scratch and scar. And so did my dedicated driver, Dedan. Driving in these conditions would stretch the capabilities of all safari drivers. Especially with the long hours that we did. But, he never complained. He surpassed his job description. He showed his loyalty. And we got to the end still sharing jokes and smiling. This was by far the most challenging , but also interesting, adventure to date. We've never been in terrain like this before. My thanks go out to him yet again....in bundles. And to our private guide for his assistance and knowledge and for also sharing the challenging times we had. Have we given up on finding this black leopard? Not likely !!! Plans are afoot for next time.......... We are both determined and focused to find it. Whatever it takes. Wherever it takes us. Documenting this beautiful creature in it's own habitat is our mission.

item.title: Meet the Newborn
item.dc:creator: robyn
item.content:encoded: It was an early morning game drive in Maasai Mara in June 2017. We had a plan to go and find a female leopard and her cub but that plan changed....as they do! There was radio notification of a giraffe giving birth. Luckily we weren't so far away and the deal was sealed...let's go and see if we can make it to her in time. I was later told that seeing such an event is a once-in-a-lifetime experience. After some pretty bumpy driving by my very adept driver, we made it to the new mother only a mere few minutes after the baby had dropped onto the ground (giraffes give birth standing). The mother was standing very still with the baby sheltered between her legs wobbling its head around in the warm morning sunshine. It took only a short time and the new baby attempted to take its first tentative steps, falling down repeatedly several times until it gained enough strength to remain standing. The mother by now, was becoming more attentive having caught her breath from the birthing. She began licking her baby and supporting its efforts to find where it needed to be to suckle. In the meantime, another male and a female had wandered along to see what was happening and to meet the newborn. Nothing unusual in that. It seemed like a natural thing to do......until... The male took a shine to the new mother just a bit more than he should have. He was a fully grown male and his initial interests were concentrated on sharing suckling duties with the baby. The new mother was not liking this attention one little bit. Still gaining her strength, she made several attempts to kick him away. She didn't move her body, only her leg. He wasn't having any of that and continued to either come between her and her baby or from the other side. At one point he even chewed on the babys ear in an attempt to pull it away from suckling the mother. This behaviour continued intermittently for about one hour. A combination of distressing the mother and annoying the somewhat confused baby. And, if that wasn't enough of the males strange behaviour, he then decided to try and mount/mate with the new mother!! That was it!!! She had had enough disturbance and he was given his marching orders. The mother body slammed the male and chased him away. Finally he took notice and wandered off with the other female to graze. The new mother went back to peacefully groom her baby while it finished feeding. The warmth from the sunshine combined with a full tummy invigorated it and very soon it, too, was walking off to begin a new life in the wilderness. If seeing a giraffe birth wasn't special enough, combining it with the male behaviour, I feel, is pretty extraordinary.

item.title: When Motherly Instinct is Greater than Killing
item.dc:creator: robyn
item.content:encoded: June 20, 2017 and we're doing a full day game drive in Kenya's Maasai Mara Reserve. No day is ever the same as the one before and the impending day certainly proved that! We came across a pride of lions that consisted of four lionesses and seven cubs of varying sizes and ages. One was just a baby. They were sitting in the open enjoying the morning sunshine. One of the lionesses spotted a lone wildebeest and crept behind trees towards it. The wildebeest, however, saw it first and took off out of sight. She sat there a wee bit disillusioned. The wildebeest had gone! And then she spotted something else....... Hidden in the bushes a short distance away and, at that point not seen by us, was a female waterbuck. The waterbuck stood rigid. So did the lioness. The lioness crept up to get a better view and stood stock still for several minutes without moving. Interestingly, so did the waterbuck. Why didn't she run? Had she not contemplated the danger or ability of this cat? She could certainly see it. For several minutes both animals eyed each other without movement. As soon as the cat made her move the waterbuck took off and we never saw her again. Did the lioness see something we couldn't? Could she smell something? Unknown to us, lying in the grass was a few-minutes-old baby waterbuck. The reason why the mother hadn't run away. She was protecting her newborn. As soon as the lioness reached it, the calfs instincts to stand kicked in. We thought, that's it. All over for the newborn. But, the lioness started to lick it. To mother it. Her own motherly instinct had taken over. Only the week before, I had been watching such a thing on TV and never imagined that I would get to witness this in real life for myself. But here it was. At times the lioness seemed a bit unsure what to do with the baby. She would pat it and push it gently. Was she trying to make it stand? She bit into its skin but not into its body. The baby was by now crying out and becoming distressed. The mother was still nowhere to be seen although I'm sure she was close enough to hear it. The crying got louder and more consistent. It was heart wrenching to watch this but there was nothing we could do. Even though the lioness picked the baby up by the throat, she still was not making any move to kill it. And still more playing. The lioness is still not sure what she should be doing with this thing. It's not reacting like a cub would do. It's not running away. In fact, at this point, the baby couldn't even stand. The baby is distressed. The lioness is confused. The killer instinct has not been lodged because the prey did not run. But, now the lioness is aware that the crying has alerted the rest of the pride and they are on their way to see what is happening. The lioness takes the baby by the throat as if she is transporting her own cub to a safer place. She is focusing on protecting her "baby". The lionesses rush in and can smell the birthing fluids in the grass. It's time for lioness #1 to make a move. The baby is still crying! Lioness #2 charges in from the side in an attempt to take away the baby waterbuck from her sister. The claws go out........... And lioness #2 takes off into the bushes with the baby waterbuck. Lioness #1 can only watch as her "baby" has been taken from her. Lioness #2 though has the baby by the skin too and not the body. We thought, ok now the baby will be put out of its misery quickly. It will be spared any further distress. These lions are hungry and this will be a meal for at least one of them. But, no.......... The lioness takes the baby up onto a mound in the bushes. The rest of the pride are not allowed near. When any of the cubs attempt to get near enough to take a bite they are met with angry growls. Enough to make them retreat. Here's where it gets even more interesting. Lioness #2 also has the motherly instinct within her. The baby is lying on the grass and she is licking it. She places both front paws over the top of the babys body to protect it from the pride. We thought it was already dead, but it wasn't. After some time, the littlest cub ventures close. It is the only one the lioness will allow to do that. Is this her own baby? Does she want to allow it to feed? The baby waterbuck is now dead and the lioness has begun to eat. She stays here for some time and seems in no hurry to devour it quickly. The rest of the pride eventually wander off nearby knowing they won't get any of the meal. Time has passed. We move away. Just then the lioness comes running out of the bushes and into long grass in the sun. She has eaten the torso of the waterbuck but it is still attached by a thin piece of skin along the spine. She sits in the grass and continues to chew on the carcass. In come the pride cubs. They're very hungry and they're going to try their luck again. The first to get too close gets a bite to the paw. The second, a young male, gets a beating and ends up upside down. Both cubs retreat. Eventually, the lioness stands up and walks off, leaving the cubs to fight over the spoils. One of the braver cubs grabs the carcass at the front. In the scramble to do so, the skin across the spine of the carcass gets wrapped around the cubs body. Two other cubs make a grab at the skin but this means their teeth are embedded in the back of the cub as well. This is obviously causing pain for the cub holding the carcass and it can't move. The two cubs at the back are not letting go either and there is a stale mate for about five minutes. Each time the cub tries to get up, even just a few centimetres, and walk off, it can't. After some minutes, the two cubs at the back relinquish their grasp and the one at the front launches forward. The young male at the back pounces on the back part of the carcass and it separates. At least another hour passes until the cubs have eaten what was left. They are now playing with the leg bones. The lionesses have wandered off. What a truly amazing sight to see. Although it was not an easy thing to watch, or to hear, as the baby waterbuck was being cajoled, it's part of nature and we are not to intervene. It's part of survival in the wild. Life ...and death!

item.title: Taking the Plunge
item.dc:creator: robyn
item.content:encoded: August 20, 2017: Maasai Mara Reserve, Kenya. I'm doing my first full day of a six day photographic safari. It's Migration season here and the big cats are finding their availability of a meal plentiful. Right now, myself and my driver, are watching a young female leopard wandering around beneath us on the banks of a narrow stream. There are pockets of water and twists and bends. It's 1200 hrs....mid day. The sun is hot. She's not particularly interested in doing anything but cranes her neck to see if any prey is about. Nope. Nothing in view here although we've seen a reedbuck around the corner which she doesn't know about. Back to the bushes she goes. We stay with her for an hour before she finds a nice sheltered spot to take a snooze. One and half hours later, and yes we sat there all that time, she emerged from her snooze and wandered off to find a drink. She crossed a scrappy, dry grass area and made her way towards a muddy waterhole. Surrounding this waterhole were some random small bushs and long, untidy grasses. Standing on the edge was a reedbuck intermittantly nibbling on the grass and looking up. It had not seen the leopard. Initially, the leopard didn't see the reedbuck either. But, then it did........... The leopard took a few very careful steps forward, stopped and engaged her sights on the reedbuck. Her timing had to be precise. She would put her head down each time the reedbuck looked up. We waited for the reedbuck to see the cat and take off. It didn't! Waiting for that moment of charge was nerve wracking. But then, the next time the reedbucks head went down, the leopard dashed through the grass. The reedbuck, on seeing her charge, took off. It appeared it may have tripped in the long grass and fell upside down. The leopard pounced! The velocity of the chase catapolted both animals downwards and into the waterhole. It wasn't possible for the leopard to latch onto the reedbucks throat because of the water so she held tight to the top of the neck. The intent being to rupture an artery or sever the spinal cord. Both of which would bring death. At that point, it didn't. The reedbuck fought the fight. At times it was quiet then it would get a burst of life and writhe around in the water trying to escape. The reedbuck screamed loud and pitifully. The efforts were futile against the power of this leopards bite. And then it went still..........! The leopard clambered backwards up the bank. The power and strength behind this cat to execute this movement, and bearing in mind its expended energy preceding this, was absolutely amazing. The reedbuck is lifeless but still not dead. Now out of the water, the leopard can get the throat stranglehold and put the reedbuck out of its misery finally. It's been an exhausting process. It's now 1440pm. Fifty minutes since the leopard first laid eyes on the reedbuck. She has gathered some semblance of breath, tried to shake off the mud from her paws and it's time to find a safe place to stash her kill. She's very particular about where she's going. Even passing by two trees along the way. One of which would have been ideal for stringing up her prey from other hungry predators. It's hot and there's more long grass and bushes to evade as she goes. Eventually she finds a gut amongst heavy bushes and stops. We wait for some time expecting her to climb a tree next to the gut but she doesn't. Out of sight, she recollects herself before proceding to disembowel the reedbuck. The following morning, there she is: belly full, relaxed and enjoying quiet time in the morning sunshine on the branch of that tree. What an AMAZING, rare spectacle to witness. She stayed in the same area over the coming days. We saw her again. Quite relaxed and happy. See you again soon beautiful cat...........!
item.excerpt:encoded: August 20, 2017: Maasai Mara Reserve, Kenya. I’m doing my first full day of a six day photographic safari . It’s Migration season here and the big cats are finding their availability of a meal plentiful.

wp:comment.wp:comment_content: This such amazing story and what great photography go Robyn
Hi Gail. Thanks muchly. Lots to talk about over a cuppa when I get back huh? :-)
Your pictures always make me feel like I am right there with you. Thanks be safe and take more pictures to share

Thanks, Zoie. You're welcome. I was very lucky to see it happen. That's what happens when you sit and wait. Even if sometimes it's for several hours. I get to see so many unusual things by doing that.

I love leopards. I know some of you felt bad for the redbuck. I wish the best for the beautiful Leopard. I rather see nature killing nature. People pay high prices for someone killing Leopards for trophy or make a coat out of the Leopard. Thank you for sharing you story and beautiful pictures.
Thanks, Theresa. I'd rather see nature killing nature too. And everything has to eat to survive.
Amazing photos
Thank you, Noeline :-)

item.title: 5-Day Kenya Safari in the Maasai Mara
item.dc:creator: daniel
item.content:encoded:
Maasai Mara Reserve would have to be the number one wilderness travel destination in Africa. It's home to the Great Wildebeest Migration where 2 million strong wildebeest and zebra migrate into the reserve following the rains. No wildlife spectacle rivals this.
But, outside of this seasonal spectacle, this park hosts an abundance of predators and plains game all year round. Here you will see real Africa. Lions, leopard, cheetah, elephants, zebra, giraffe, hippo… there is a diverse array of wild animals in Maasai Mara. Your 5 day safari is focused entirely on finding the best wildlife sightings within this Reserve. No two days are the same.

wp:postmeta.wp:meta_value:
We depart Nairobi after breakfast and make our way to the world famous Maasai Mara Reserve. We’ll make a stop along the way at the viewing point over looking the expansive Great Rift Valley.
Our next break is in Narok for a comfort stop/coffee before our final leg to the Reserve. We will arrive at our lodge for a sumptuous lunch before time to relax for the afternoon. You might want a dip in the pool or sit in the shade with a good book.
At 4pm we head off on our first game drive into the park to seek out lions, leopard, cheetah, elephants or anything out there that wants to be seen. As the sun sets, we’ll arrive back at our lodge for hot showers and dinner.
Later, lay your head on your pillow and wait for the sounds of lions calling their pride or hyenas cackling as you drift off to sleep. Lala vizuri!

Each day we depart the lodge after our yummy breakfast and spend a full day of safari game viewing. We will go where the best wildlife sightings are and explore different areas as we go.
There is no set plan as this is an uncharted adventure. We’ll get you where you need to be on any given day depending on what is happening. And, if you have a special animal you really would like to see, we’ll do our very best to find it for you.
As the day progresses, we stop under a shady tree for morning tea, a packed picnic lunch and then afternoon tea later as we wind down our exploring before heading back to our lodge in the early evening.

The time has come to leave and make our way back to the city life. We’ll make our comfort stop in Narok as we go and arrive back in Nairobi for cafe lunch. You’ll then be taken back to your post safari accommodation for a well earned siesta.
The range of animals and birds we saw over the 5 days had to be seen to be believed.

item.title: 7-Day Kenya Safari Package
item.dc:creator: daniel
item.content:encoded: Our 7 day package gives a taste of Kenya for those who don't have the luxury of time. There's still a large concentration of birds and animals though. Perhaps you're on a business trip with some days spare? Or maybe a local who hasn't seen the country or been to Maasai Mara? Let us show you!

wp:postmeta.wp:meta_value:
After breakfast we leave Nairobi and make our way towards Lake Elementaita. We will make a brief stop at the escarpment overlooking the majestic Great Rift Valley.
We will arrive at Elementaita in time for lunch and your afternoon can be spent relaxing. There’s a pool overlooking the expanse of the lake or you may feel like a massage. Pelicans and flamingos go about their daily hustle right outside your room. Early mornings are a good time to catch the flamingos flying in. Enjoy!

We head off after breakfast, with our picnic lunch, to do a full day game drive in Nakuru National Park. This park is renowned for having over 400 bird species. Lions and leopard live here too and hunt out buffalo and zebra. Both black and white rhino can be seen along with the Rothschild giraffe. The only park where this giraffe can be seen in the wild.
We’ll head back to Elementaita in the late afternoon so you can relax before dinner with a cold beverage overlooking the beautiful lake.

We’ll leave the lake shore this morning and head off to the famous Maasai Mara Reserve arriving for lunch at our lodge. It’s then chill out time before our 4pm game drive. We’ll head out into the park and see what we can find... maybe a pride of lions or a leopard eyeing up a gazelle?
As the sun dips deeper on to the horizon we’ll make our way inside the lodge grounds for our evening relaxation. There’s time for a hot shower and a cold vino before dinner before tucking up in bed to listen to the sounds of the wild. Good night!

Each day is spent full day game driving. After a hearty breakfast to keep us going, we’ll explore the wonders of this park seeking out the best wildlife sightings for you. Each day is different and we’ll explore a different area each time.
Our prime objective is to find the animals for you to enjoy. We’ll get in the best position possible for great photos without encroaching on the animals comfort and safety. We’ll make this your ultimate safari experience!
At the end of each day it’s back to the lodge to chill out and remember the magic of your discovery.

We bid farewell to our home for the past few days and head back to the bustle of the city. We’ll stop briefly in Narok to stretch our legs and have a comfort stop over coffee. A welcome cafe lunch ends our safari before dropping you back at your post safari accommodation.

What impressed me most about travelling in Kenya with Robyn is how capable and meticulous she is at organising safari trips and how informed she is about African wildlife and the various national parks that are on her itinerary.

item.title: 10-Day Kenya Safari Package
item.dc:creator: daniel
item.content:encoded: Our 10 Day Package begins with full on exposure to bird life. Lake Naivasha, Lake Elementaita and Lake Nakuru are abundant with so many species of birds. A highlight, of course, being flamingos. The second part is all about the animals. The big cats; lions, leopards and cheetahs. The elephants and buffalos. Giraffes and gazelles. Are you ready to explore?

wp:postmeta.wp:meta_value: We leave Nairobi after breakfast and make our way northward to the Ol Pejeta Conservancy where we arrive for lunch. Time then to relax before an afternoon game drive at 4pm. There’s a waterhole right outside your room where an abundance of animals gather to drink. Even the rhinos! Here is the only place where you can do an optional night game drive.

After breakfast we make our way to the Aberdares. Our lunch today will be at the Aberdare Country Club; a sister to the lodge where we will stay overnight. We will take with us an overnight bag only. Our main luggage will be held in locked storage at the Country Club until our return tomorrow morning.
We board a bus at 2.30pm which takes us 45 min to our accommodation within the Aberdare National Park. Here we will observe the wildlife at close range from one of four viewing decks or a cosy lounge chair. There is a dedicated photo hide on the lower deck where you are able to take close up uninhibited photography.

We leave the Ark Lodge at 8am on the bus and drive out of the park and back to Aberdare Country Club. If we get lucky and see animals before exiting the park we will make a stop. Leopards are often seen at this time.
At ACC we collect our main luggage and get on our way to our next destination. Along the way we stop at the Equator for a water demonstration. Morning tea stop is at Thompson Falls (named after the explorer who discovered the Aberdare Mountains and named them after his employer, Lord Aberdare; and who has the Thompson gazelle named after him). Arrive at Lake Elementaita for lunch. Afternoon to relax and take in the view and birdlife.

We head off after breakfast, with our picnic lunch, to do a full day game drive in Nakuru National Park. This park is renowned for having over 400 bird species. Lions and leopard live here too and hunt out buffalo and zebra. Both black and white rhino can be seen along with the Rothschild giraffe. The only park where this giraffe can be seen in the wild.
We’ll head back to Elementaita in the late afternoon so you can relax before dinner with a cold beverage overlooking the beautiful lake.

We’ll leave the lake shore this morning and head off to the famous Maasai Mara Reserve arriving for lunch at our lodge. It’s then chill out time before our 4pm game drive. We’ll head out into the park and see what we can find... maybe a pride of lions or a leopard eyeing up a gazelle?
As the sun dips deeper on to the horizon we’ll make our way inside the lodge grounds for our evening relaxation. There’s time for a hot shower and a cold vino before dinner before tucking up in bed to listen to the sounds of the wild. Good night!

Each day is spent full day game driving. After a hearty breakfast to keep us going, we’ll explore the wonders of this park seeking out the best wildlife sightings for you. Each day is different and we’ll explore a different area each time.
Our prime objective is to find the animals for you to enjoy. We’ll get in the best position possible for great photos without encroaching on the animals comfort and safety. We’ll make this your ultimate safari experience!
At the end of each day it’s back to the lodge to chill out and remember the magic of your discovery.
I gained an appreciation for the ‘law of nature’ within the animal kingdom, and a respect for the people that I met along the way.

item.content:encoded: So you want a bit more than a few days on safari? You're wanting to see more of the country? Then look no further than our two week adventure. There's loads to see here and a super special treat visiting the only two remaining Northern White Rhinos on this Earth. Jump on board and let's go see what wants to be seen.

item.title: 21 Day Package
item.dc:creator: daniel
item.content:encoded: Now this is the ultimate of the ultimate!! Three weeks taking in ten different locations. Each place completely different to the next which gives you so much variety both in wildlife and landscape. The opportunities for photography and making memories are boundless. This package is fine tuned to make sure you don't burn out and comes with plenty of flexibility. Are you up for the challenge?

wp:postmeta.wp:meta_value:
It’s a long drive today to our destination but there’s lots of culture to see along the way. We’ll make a stop for morning tea as we go and arrive at our lodge for a late lunch. After lunch you can leap into your own private plunge pool outside your tent and watch the wild animals pass by.
What a way to start a safari! Relax! Wine and dine over looking the lodge waterhole.

It’s a full day game drive exploring the park. We take our morning tea on top of Mudanda Rock where we get a great view for miles. Tsavo is generally a hot, dry area so the waterholes within the park are where we’re most likely to find animals. The big cats are here along with the “ red elephants” who get their colour from the red earth found in this area.
Picnic lunch at a campsite followed by more seeking of wildlife. It’s back to the waterhole outside our lodge to enjoy a cold drink before dinner.

It’s a cruisy drive to get to Tsavo West. We arrive at the park entrance for morning tea before venturing inside and visiting Mzima Springs for a short guided walk. Here you might get lucky and see hippo and crocs.
Onward to the lodge for lunch. This gorgeous lodge overlooks an elevated waterhole where, at certain times of the year, it is teeming with wildlife. Afternoon game drive. Take in the floodlit waterhole as you enjoy your cold beverage before dinner.

As we depart the park we will pass through the Shetani lava flow. This flow is 8km long and 1.6 km wide and was formed by an eruption only 200 years ago. You can get out and take a little stroll for a photo if you choose. We do a game drive from the lodge up to this point.
Arriving for lunch at our next lodge we now have a magnificent view of Mt Kilimanjaro (weather permitting). Our afternoon game drive takes us into the park where it is starkly different to where we have been. Amboseli is flat and open plains. There is an abundance of bird life and it is renown for the elephants that frequent the swamp areas. Flamingos have recently taken up home here too.
After breakfast we head off on a full day game drive in Amboseli National Park. Let’s go see what wants to be seen! Will Mt Kili be shining for us today?

We make our way back to the outskirts of Nairobi. After lunch we can relax before our evening dinner and Safari Catz SOUND AND DANCE show. Highly energetic, highly entertaining and one of the many highlights of your itinerary. In the meantime you can explore the expansive grounds of our hotel.

We leave Nairobi after breakfast and make our way northward to the Ol Pejeta Conservancy where we arrive for lunch. Time then to relax before an afternoon game drive at 4pm. Here is the only place where you can do an optional night game drive.There’s a waterhole right outside your room where an abundance of animals gather to drink. Even the rhinos!

After breakfast we visit the only two remaining Northern White Rhino on this earth. Return to camp with short game drive on the way. Lunch and afternoon to relax before another afternoon game drive. You have the opportunity to visit Jane Goodall's chimpanzee sanctuary if you wish.​​There are 32 individual wild dogs here and you might get lucky enough to spot them hunting.

It’s a transit day to Samburu on good, easy roads. We check in at the park entrance then do a game drive en route to the lodge. Samburu is dry, arid land with rocky formations surrounding the Ewaso Nyiro River which runs alongside our home for the next two nights.
Lunch then relax until our afternoon game drive. ​As you relax, you listen to the mellow sounds of running water beneath the shady trees. Ahhhh bliss...!

Today is split into morning and afternoon game drives as the animals tend to hide from the hot mid day sun. In Samburu you have the opportunity to see grevy zebra, somali ostrich, gerenuk, vulturine guinea fowl and beisa oryx which you will not see in other places. The big cats prowl here too along with an abundance of bird life. Resident leopards can be seen just outside the lodge along with elephants.

We’re on the road again and make our way to the Aberdares. Our lunch today will be at the Aberdare Country Club; a sister to the lodge where we will stay overnight. We will take with us an ​overnight bag only​. Our main luggage will be held in locked storage at the Country Club until our return tomorrow morning.
We board a bus at 2.30pm which takes us 45 min to our accommodation within the Aberdare National Park. Here we will observe the wildlife at close range from one of four viewing decks or a cosy lounge chair. There is a dedicated photo hide on the lower deck where you are able to take close up, uninhibited photography.

After breakfast we leave the Ark Lodge at 8am on the bus and drive out of the park and back to Aberdare Country Club. If we get lucky and see animals before exiting the park we will make a stop. Leopards are often seen at this time.
At ACC we collect our main luggage and get on our way to our next destination. Along the way we stop at the Equator for a water demonstration. Morning tea stop is at Thompson Falls (named after the explorer who discovered the Aberdare Mountains and named them after his employer, Lord Aberdare; and who has the Thompson gazelle named after him).
Arrive at Lake Naivasha for lunch. Our afternoon is spent relaxing in the expansive 150 acre grounds of our accommodation. A resident giraffe, waterbuck, vervet and colobus monkeys wander around freely. Free time to enjoy!

After breakfast in Naivasha, we will be dropped off at the lakeside to enjoy a one and half hour boat ride around the lake. Our captain will provide bait fish to entice the mighty African Fish Eagle down from the tree tops. This freshwater lake is home to a wide variety of birds and a large population of hippo. You might even get to see the resident python lazing in the sunshine amongst the foliage.
After our boat ride, we’ll make a drive to Lake Elementaita and to our lodge for lunch. Afternoon to relax, take a swim in the pool or just listen to the birdlife.

Today we enjoy a full day game drive around the shores of Lake Nakuru. This is the only place you will be able to see the endangered Rothschild giraffe in its own habitat. White and black rhino also live here along with many other wildlife species.
We take a picnic lunch with us and depart the park in the afternoon making our way back to Lake Elementaita and the relaxed atmosphere on the waters’ edge.

We leave Elementaita after breakfast and make our way to the world famous Maasai Mara National Reserve. We stop along the way for a stretch and coffee break before arriving at the Reserve for a late lunch. ​There’s time to chill out before your afternoon game drive going in search of wild things.​​

As the sun sets, we’ll arrive back at our lodge for hot showers and dinner. Later, lay your head on your pillow and wait for the sounds of lions calling their pride or hyenas cackling as you drift off to sleep. Lala vizuri!

We’ll make this your ultimate safari experience!
At the end of each day it’s back to the lodge to chill out and remember the magic of your discovery.

item.title: Takedown in Tsavo
item.dc:creator: robyn
item.content:encoded: Warning: this video contains graphic images of animal behaviour. It was June 1st 2014 and my driver and I arrived at a waterhole in Tsavo East NP, Kenya. It was around 7.30am and three zebras were drinking. Without warning and within seconds, a lioness shot out from behind a bush and leapt onto the back of one of the zebras. The other two took off in opposite directions. At one point both the lioness and the zebra were both airborne. They then crashed down into the water where there was a struggle. The lioness got the zebra by the neck but could not cover the windpipe with her mouth because that would mean putting her own mouth into the water. For that reason the struggle lasted ten long minutes. During that time the zebra lost all energy and its mouth went beneath the surface of the water and drowned. A juvenile male had come to assist the lioness but was ineffective as he was more concerned with keeping clean. Hovering around the edge of the waterhole was the rest of the pride of eight. After some time, some of the pride managed to drag the body to the water's edge and the meal began. Within thirty hours there was nothing left but the skull. The elephants then came and chased the pride away.
item.excerpt:encoded: It was June 1st 2014 and my driver and I arrived at a waterhole in Tsavo East NP, Kenya. It was around 7.30am and three zebras were drinking. Without warning and within seconds, a lioness shot out from behind a bush and leapt onto the back of one of the zebras.

item.title: "Take Me To The Mara To See The Lions"
item.dc:creator: robyn
item.content:encoded:
In 2009, I got big and brave and made my first journey to the African continent. I was travelling solo so decided to go on an overlanding truck where I would be with other people and everything was organised. Plus, safety was paramount. One portion of this journey was from Capetown, South Africa, right up to Nairobi in Kenya.
On this adventure, I met Loes, a lady from Holland who would come to be a special friend. She, too, was travelling solo. Maybe that's why we connected as we did. Over the weeks of travel we laughed a lot and shared life experiences. She told me she had just finished treatment for cancer and this was her treat to herself. Her father had not long died of cancer and she wanted to make the most of life.
Along the way I came to learn the special places that inspired her the most and, at times, I would see her taking quiet moments on a river bank or under a tree somewhere. I thought, at those times, she was most likely thinking about her health, her life, and her Dad. I let her be. Sometimes she would wander off on her own and take photos of beautiful things or places then we'd chat about them later. She particularly liked sunrises and sunsets.
The overland trip ended in Nairobi. I had plans to stay another seven days and join another company to see a bit of this new country. Loes was going back to Holland the following day - a decision she came to regret! She wasn't needing to go back to work so it would have been easy to change her flight and stay another week. It wasn't talked about at that point so we said our goodbyes as she was leaving early the following morning for the airport.
I continued my safari in Kenya which included two nights in Maasai Mara. For whatever reason, I felt I had been there before even though it was, in reality, my first time. I declared then I would return to this magic place (and now, of course, it is like my second home).
When I returned home to New Zealand, Loes and I continued to keep in contact on Skype. I raved about how beautiful the Mara was and she was kicking herself that she didn't stay and join me. We declared that we would make a plan and go back together one day. She kept up with her regular medical tests to make sure she remained in good health.
In 2010, Loes decided to come and visit me in New Zealand and see the country I lived in. She wanted to see the world and do as much as she could. She travelled the length of the country from the bottom to the top. I was with her for the bulk of that. On our overland trip in Africa, we had also met two kiwi women who we spent some time with. One was living in Wellington so we stopped off and visited with her and reminisced about Africa. The other was in Australia so we had planned to fly there for a week after our trip around New Zealand was finished. This we did, and she got to see and experience a bit of that country too. Loes parted company there and flew back to Holland. I flew back to New Zealand.
Later that same year, our kiwi friend in Australia won a photo competition that was being run by the overlanding company we had travelled with together. The prize was a trip of her choice that the company offered. She invited me to accompany her - which I did. We went back to South Africa and did a safari from Johannesburg, up to Kruger and finishing in Capetown. We added on a two week wildlife conservation course at a private reserve before flying back home. I recall mentioning how Loes would have loved being there too.
Once we were home, we both kept in contact with Loes in Holland. We came to learn in 2011 that her cancer had returned and she was again needing invasive treatment. I followed her journey through conversations on Skype and we uplifted our prior conversation about planning that safari in Kenya together and, especially, to the Mara. She constantly regretted not going with me in 2009. She had hoped all would be well and the treatment would work as it did the first time.
It didn't !!
The conversations had come to an abrupt end and I feared getting the email from her girlfriend that she had died. I got that email. In it the friend shared Loes's last days before her passing. Two days prior, Loes's friends had pushed her, in her wheelchair, outside into the sun and asked her "Where would you like to go?".
Loes replied, "Take me to the Mara to see the lions". That was her final wish!
You can imagine the heartbreak!
In 2012, the following year, I came to win a competition run by that same overlanding company in Africa that we had originally met. Was it coincidence that my prize ended up being the exact same trip that Loes and I had done in 2009?
Through Loes's friend in Holland, I sent a message to her family requesting that perhaps I may be able to have some of her ashes to take back to Africa. I knew her family spoke no English so couldn't contact them directly. And I didn't know what their beliefs were in regard to ashes after cremation.
Time passed with no word so I believed that nothing would be forthcoming. I set about getting organised for my trip. Just days before I was to leave, a package arrived in my mailbox. It was the ashes !! I carefully placed them in a special part of my luggage and told no one - fearing they may be taken off me.
And so the safari throughout Africa began- that very trip Loes and I had first met and done together . When we came to the places where I knew she had enjoyed the most, I would wait for everyone to get off the truck and go exploring and I would hang back so I could get the ashes out of my bag. I would place a small portion in the palm of my hand and take a photo with the backdrop included. My intention was to, at the end, send the images back to her family. The family had sent me a copy of her funeral sheet so I did the same images with that. Later, these images became a treasure for her family and I was told they couldn't stop crying.
I did this right through the countries we had visited - South Africa, Namibia, Botswana, Zimbabwe, Zambia, Malawi, Tanzania to Kenya. I recall sitting at a waterhole in Etosha, in Namibia, one evening. I had decided this would be one of her special places as we had both spent quite some time there together. At the specific time I scattered her ashes, a breeze blew up from nowhere. I knew she was there!
But, because she hadn't visited any of Kenya, I had purposely kept the last portion of ashes for the Mara. I had to find a special place. It wasn't easy as I had to find somewhere where Loes would be able to see the lions and where she would have an unspoilt view across the plains. I only had a set number of days and I had to get it right.
I finally found that place - under this tree. Loes can see all the animals. She can see a vast, open view. She can see the birds. She can see her sunrises and sunsets. So, here I scattered the last remaining ashes.
Whenever I go to Mara and stay near that tree, I pass each morning and say Hi to her. Then give thanks for my day when we pass back in the evening. Last year was the first time I had stopped for picnic lunch under that tree. I sat at the back of the van in the quiet. Loes had a bird she particularly liked - the Lilac Breasted Roller. One of these same birds flew into the tree and sat on the branch above my head chirping. At the same time, a breeze came from nowhere. I knew she was there.
So, my friend - we made our trip.
I took you to the Mara to see the lions!

item.title: Go East: Amboseli, Tsavo & Eastern Kenya Safari
item.dc:creator: robyn
item.content:encoded: NEW !! This is our latest safari itinerary inclusion packed with extra activities on top of our game drives. Twelve exciting days out in the wild but concentrating on the eastern parks in Kenya – Amboseli, Tsavo West, Taita Hills, Tsavo East, Lumo Conservancy and back to Amboseli. Add in night game drives, visit Shatani Lava Flow and Mzima Springs, underground photography hides, sundowners, bush dinner, bush breakfast, cultural village visit,overnight in a photography hide fully kitted out with beds and dedicated outdoor lighting on the waterhole. What an experience!

wp:postmeta.wp:meta_value:
We make our way out of the city and towards the acclaimed Amboseli NP, home of elephant herds and at the foot of Mount Kilimanjaro -Africas’ highest mountain and the highest free standing mountain in the world. We relax after lunch before our afternoon game drive where we will go in search of big cats, elephants, zebras……….
MEAL PLAN: full board ACCOMMODATION: SERENA AMBOSELI LODGE

AMBOSELI TO TSAVO WEST

(distance 120 km )

Once we enter the gate into Tsavo West NP, we begin our game drive towards our hotel. We will pass through the Shatani Lava Flow .The black lava is spread over 50 km. The name “Shetani,” which means “devil” in Swahili, is derived from the local belief that when the lava flow first occurred, around 500 years ago, it was the work of evil spirits due to the violent and fiery eruption. We’ll also visit the Mzima Springs which produce an incredible 250 million litres of fresh water daily. We’ll do a guided walk which includes going into an underwater viewing chamber. After lunch at our lodge, and rest time, we will head off on our afternoon game drive.
MEAL PLAN: full board ACCOMMODATION: KILAGUNI SERENA LODGE

TSAVO WEST TO TAITA HILLS

(distance 90 km )

The private Taita Hills Wildlife Sanctuary is our next destination. Our accommodation is famed for being one of the worlds’ most photographed lodges. The sanctuary is home to more than 50 different species of animals and over 300 different species of birds. There is also a tunnel that leads to an “all day” underground photo hide where all manner of animals come to drink at the well- positioned waterhole outside it. Today we will do both an afternoon and night game drive. Night drives provide an opportunity of seeing animals not encountered during the day eg/ striped hyena, mongoose, civet, genet, porcupine and bushbaby. And maybe get lucky to see predators hunting.
MEAL PLAN: full board ACCOMMODATION : SAROVA SALT LICK LODGE
Transport - 4x4 safari vehicle with pop up roof
Park entry fees- for all parks listed in the itinerary
All activities at Lumo as listed ( bush breakfast, cultural visit, photo hide)
Any other item not listed above
Thank you for making our trip so special, I couldn't recommend (and I do often) your safari highly enough. Each day just got better than the last.

Todays activities include both a morning and afternoon game drive. This will provide an ideal opportunity to see the abundant wildlife that resides here. In the latter part of our afternoon drive we will head to one of the four bush activity venues within the sanctuary for sundowners (drinks as the sun sets) overlooking the magnificent views of the Taita Hills. This is followed by the awesome experience of dinner out in the bush. After dinner we can do a night drive back to our lodge.
MEAL PLAN: full board SAROVA SALT LICK LODGE

TAITA HILLS TO TSAVO EAST

(distance 90 km )

We leave after breakfast and head to our next location - Tsavo East NP, famous for its large herds of red- dusted elephants. This is the largest, and oldest, National Park in Kenya covering almost 14,000 sq km. It’s also the home of the longest plateau in the world - Yatta Plateau. There is abundant wildlife and birds in this park. The critically endangered Hirola Antelope resides here but it’s not easy to find them.
MEAL PLAN : full board ACCOMMODATION : ASHNIL ARUBA LODGE

After breakfast we’ll head off, with picnic lunch, for a full day game drive. Depending on time and what we see, morning tea will be on top of Mudanda Rock. Mudanda rock dates back to the Precambrian era, it is said to have been used for drying strips of meat and as a lookout in the past by the local tribes. Today it serves as one of the view spots with the top giving 360deg views of the park.
MEAL PLAN: full board ACCOMMODATION : ASHNIL ARUBA LODGE

TSAVO EAST TO LUMO CONSERVANCY

(distance 100 km )

We’ll arrive at our next destination in plenty of time for lunch, rest, then an afternoon game drive to explore this region. This conservancy is very community minded and has made tangible improvements to the lives of the local people with investments in infrastructure, education and healthcare. It’s also an inspiring example of how people and wildlife can co-exist. Afternoon game drive and night game drive for those that want. ( night game drive to be organised and paid for at the lodge)
MEAL PLAN : full board ACCOMMODATION : SOROI CHEETAH TENTED CAMP

We’ll leave the lodge at 6.30am for a morning game drive as the sun rises. This is a beautiful, peaceful time of the day when the air is cool and the predators are still active. This will culminate with a bush breakfast somewhere out in the wild. Our chef will prepare a cooked breakfast while we relax and soak up the atmosphere of the bush. This will be followed by a cultural visit to a local village. We will enter a typical ethnic home to see how they live. Other activities may include milking a cow, harvesting vegetables, traditional cooking practices, making sisal ropes, basket weaving, dancing/drumming, learning about medicinal plants. We may be driven to explore skull caves and untouched rainforest where it is possible to see rare birds and butterflies that only exist here. This will be a tailored visit to suit the group size, ensuring a personalized and engaging experience. Lunch will be back at the lodge followed by rest time. 15 minutes from the lodge is a dedicated underground, photographic hide. It is airconditioned, wifi, mini bar and tea/coffee facilities, 4 bunk beds, toilet, adjustable exterior lights and one way glass so the animals are unaware we’re there. For those that want, and dependant on numbers, we have an overnight stay at the hide.
MEAL PLAN: full board ACCOMMODATION : SOROI CHEETAH TENTED CAMP

Today we concentrate on the animals and birds with both a morning and afternoon game drive. We’ll do a PM at the photographic hide from sunset. This is the best time to get low and close to the animals as they come in to drink after a hot day.
MEAL PLAN : full board ACCOMMODATION : SOROI CHEETAH TENTED CAMP

After breakfast we leave Lumo Conservancy and head back to Amboseli in time for our lunch at the lodge. Our accommodation is just outside the park gates. Afternoon game drive.
MEAL PLAN : full board ACCOMMODATION : SENTRIM AMBOSELI

After breakfast, and with our picnic lunch, we enter the park for a full day exploring the swamps and observing the habits of the elephants, buffaloes, zebras and even lions and cheetahs if we’re lucky. We’ll head to Observation Hill to get a birds eye view of the landscape around us and Mt Kilimanjaro in all her glory. There’s an abundance of bird life in the wet areas with massive numbers of flamingoes.
MEAL PLAN : full board ACCOMMODATION : SENTRIM AMBOSELI

We’re back on the road again after breakfast heading to the city life of Nairobi. Arrive for lunch (own cost). Our overnight stay is amongst the beautiful, manicured gardens of our hotel which is set on 50 acres. Relax, swim, wander the gardens. It doesn’t end there though because tonight we enjoy a meal of a vast array of bbq meats, sizzling hot and presented on skewers and carved at our table within the atmosphere of the Nyama Choma Ranch. Live music emanates while we dine. This restaurant has its own stage, state -of-the-art lighting and sound system which will be the backdrop for a 45 minute extravaganza show of dance,brilliant costumes and acrobatics by world renown Safari Catz- a team of professionally trained and choreographed dancers. This ends our time together on safari.
MEAL PLAN : dinner and breakfast ACCOMMODATION : SAFARI PARK HOTEL
DEPARTURE DAY We will transfer you from Safari Park Hotel to the airport for your onward flight. If your flight is at night there are options available within the city limits to do extra activities (at own cost) before heading to the airport. Asante sana (thankyou very much) Karibu tena (welcome again)
Sundowner and bush dinner at Taita Hills
Driver/guide Allowances- including park fees for driver and vehicle
Insurance - medical evacuation by AMREF Flying Doctors
Farewell dinner and show at Safari Park Hotel
Twelve action-packed days across Amboseli, Tsavo West, Tsavo East, Taita Hills and Lumo Conservancy — night drives, photography hides, bush dinners and more with Robyn Preston.

item.title: Black Leopard Safari - In Search of Giza, Kenya's Melanistic Leopard
item.dc:creator: robyn
item.content:encoded: NEW !! Six awesome days of adventure concentrating on seeing the rare black leopard! We are offering you the chance of a lifetime ! Being in the presence of one of the rarest creatures on Earth - the melanistic (black) leopard is something you will always remember. The setting is in one of the remotest regions in Kenya so the numbers of humans around on any given day is very restricted. As are vehicle numbers. The only drivers permitted to do game drives here are the drivers employed by the camp. And there are strict rules around time spent with the cat to ensure she is not in any way stressed. So, this is a completely different experience but one not to be missed !! Time spent within the camp area has a family feel to it where all guests sit around one big table to eat delicious food . Pre dinner the fire pit is where we can meet people from other parts of the world and share the days' events. It's a small camp dedicated to togetherness. Just an awesome place to stay !!

wp:postmeta.wp:meta_value: Laikipia Wilderness Camp is all about adventure. It stands in one of the remotest regions of Kenya. It has become famous for sightings of the melastic (black) leopard which has her territory right around the camp. These cats are extremely rare and you will be very privileged to see one. The most famous of all, Giza, was born and raised less than 1km from camp and is especially relaxed around the vehicles. She is a wild animal and can be unpredictable so there is, as with all wild animals, no guarantee of seeing her. Although, with a six day safari, the chances are favourable. There are at least three other black leopards seen in this conservancy. The number of vehicles (3) and the time spent with Giza is limited. We will, therefore, have a private Black Leopard Vehicle which will give us priority. The leopard is respected at all sightings and game drives seeing her can be ceased if it is seen she is under any stress or needs to hunt. Game drives to see her are restricted between 6am and 8 pm so that during night hours she is left to be a leopard.
Accommodations - Holiday Inn Hotel (Nairobi - pre and post safari) B&B
Insurance : Medical evacuation by AMREF Flying Doctors
Activities at LWC - game drives, night drives, walking safari, wild dog tracking, bush meals, sundowners,
Any other item not listed above

For me, my heart sang every day just to be amongst beautiful people, new friends and of course to have the privilege of spending time with the most beautiful animals on this earth in their kingdom, long may they survive.

The daily schedule is flexible but an early start is encouraged. Tea/coffee will be served at the main tent at approx 5.30- 6am along with a light breakfast. We head out as the sun rises. Morning coffee and a muffin are served somewhere out in the bush mid morning before returning to camp around 11am for a scrummy lunch. Sometimes lunch may be served out in the wild. The afternoon is the hottest time of the day - even for the animals, who will hide in the shade- so we will stay in camp to rest until 4pm before enjoying a freshly baked cake with tea/coffee before heading off again for the afternoon/night game drive. Night game drives can also unearth other unusual species such as striped hyena, aardwolf, aardvark, zorilla, porcupine, genet and other small mammals. Sundowners are served in the vehicle as we wait for Giza to appear. We round off our day at 8 pm, back at camp, with drinks and chat around the fire pit before a delicious dinner is served at the communal table. It’s a real family atmosphere. Or sometimes we will stay out and enjoy a bush dinner around a fire pit in the wilderness. Lastly, it’s time for bed while listening to the sounds of the night time wildlife.

Game drives are the best way to cover ground and see the most wildlife. This area has excellent populations of elephant, reticulated giraffe, Grevy’s zebra, common zebra, warthog, buffalo, hippo and many antelope species. Lions, leopards and wild dogs are also often seen. We have 10 game drives within these six days at Laikipia Wilderness Camp before we head back to Nairobi and to your post safari accommodation. Departure We will transfer you from Holiday Inn Hotel to the airport for your onward flight. If your flight is at night there are options available within the city limits to do extra activities (at own cost) before heading to the airport. Asante sana (thankyou very much) Karibu tena (welcome again).
Black Leopard Safari Kenya | Laikipia Wilderness - REP Kenya Safaris
Track Giza, Kenya's famous melanistic black leopard, on a 6-day private safari in Laikipia — with night drives, walking safaris and wild dog tracking. From USD $5,208 pp.
